name: Treating sinus infection for breath

lead: Some people attribute bad breath to chronic sinus infection or post-nasal drip, the sensation of mucus draining down the throat. The goal is fresher breath by clearing the nasal source of odour.

Mucus and bacteria in infected sinuses may produce odorous compounds, and post-nasal drip is said to contribute to coating on the tongue, which is the main source of oral bad breath. Reference sources list bad breath as a symptom of sinusitis, and note that gold-standard breath testing has not been used to check whether treating chronic sinus disease improves it.

paras: Care includes saline nasal irrigation, topical decongestants, antibiotics in selected cases and, for persistent disease, endoscopic sinus surgery. It is often combined with tongue cleaning and regular oral hygiene.

Decongestant sprays are not recommended beyond about three days because of rebound congestion. Antibiotics have side effects, and most acute sinusitis is viral so they are generally not recommended for mild early cases. Surgery carries standard operative risks.

angle.text: People treat sinusitis and post-nasal drip to remove a nasal source of breath odour and the tongue coating drip can feed. Nasal sources are recognised in principle, though breath-analysis trials of this link have not been done.

lead: Treating a sinus infection or post-nasal drip for breath means applying standard sinus and nasal care, such as saline rinses, decongestants, antibiotics where indicated or surgery for persistent disease, in the hope of clearing a nasal source of bad breath. The looks and social payoff people cite is fresher breath, which affects how close others are comfortable standing and how confident the person feels talking up close.[1][2]

Sinusitis is inflammation of the nasal sinuses. Wikipedia lists bad breath among its symptoms, alongside facial pain, congestion and discoloured nasal discharge.[1] In the halitosis literature, nasal odour is said to arise from sinus infection or foreign bodies, and halitosis is often described as a symptom of chronic rhinosinusitis, though the halitosis article states that gold-standard breath analysis has not been applied to test this.[2]

Post-nasal drip, the sensation of mucus draining down the throat, is linked to rhinosinusitis, allergic and non-allergic rhinitis, acid reflux and colds.[3] It is said to contribute to tongue coating, which is itself the main source of oral halitosis, but no study quantifying this is cited; roughly 85 to 90 percent of genuine halitosis is attributed to causes within the mouth.[2] No trial testing sinus treatment for breath outcomes was found.

paras: Wikipedia describes acute sinusitis symptoms as including bad breath, congestion and green nasal discharge, and chronic sinusitis as mainly nasal obstruction with subtler pain and fever.[1] The halitosis article attributes some nasal odour to sinus infections or foreign bodies, citing Rosenberg and Scully, but says no gold-standard breath analysis has examined chronic rhinosinusitis as a cause.[2]

Post-nasal drip has several recognised causes including rhinosinusitis, allergic rhinitis, reflux and colds, and its treatment depends on the cause: antibiotics for bacterial sinusitis, allergen avoidance, antihistamines or nasal steroids for allergic rhinitis, and sometimes acid-suppressing medication.[3]

Wikipedia reports that most cases are viral and resolve without antibiotics, and that antibiotics are generally not recommended for mild or moderate disease in the first week. If symptoms last beyond 10 days, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate is considered reasonable, and the 2012 IDSA guideline recommends amoxicillin-clavulanate as the initial choice.[1] A 2018 Cochrane review found no evidence that symptoms lasting seven or more days reliably indicate bacterial infection.[1]

Nasal irrigation can help relieve congestion, with tentative evidence in acute sinusitis. Topical decongestants give temporary relief and are not recommended for more than three days, because oxymetazoline overuse can cause rebound sinusitis. Nasal steroid sprays are described as no better than placebo for unconfirmed acute sinusitis, with small benefit in confirmed cases. Endoscopic sinus surgery is considered for chronic or recurrent disease that has not responded to medication.[1]

On T Nation, a 2002 thread on sinus infections includes a poster recommending salt-water therapy, saying it did not cure their asthma but eased their symptoms.[4] In another thread a lifter hoping to reduce chronic infections and breathe through the nose again describes mouth breathing as a hardship after nasal procedures.[5] These posts concern nasal health generally and do not report breath odour results.

No studies found. No trial was located measuring bad breath outcomes after sinusitis or post-nasal drip treatment. Sinusitis trial evidence concerns nasal symptoms and infection cure rates, not breath odour.[1][2]
